title: PM10 next-hour prediction - Beijing, Aotizhongxin station (UCI)
summary: We predicted PM10 one hour ahead using the Beijing, Aotizhongxin station (UCI) data. XGBoost did best on the validation period, so we used it. On the test period (12 May 2016 to 28 Feb 2017) its average error was 14.365 µg/m³. Just repeating the last hour's value gave 14.962 µg/m³, so the model was 4.0% better. 186 episodes were flagged: 129 look like unusual pollution, 6 look like data problems and 51 are unclear. Its prediction was within 20% of the real value in 64% of the test hours. No sign of overfitting: the error on new data is close to the error on the data it learned from, once you allow for the test period being 23% easier to predict.
how_it_was_made: Read the hourly data and treated empty cells and -200 as missing.

Built the inputs: hour, weekday, the reading 1 hour before, the reading 2 hours before, the reading 3 hours before, the reading at the same time the day before, temperature, air pressure, dew point, rain, wind speed.
Split the timeline in order: first 60% to train, next 20% to choose the model, last 20% to test.
Tried Linear Regression, Random Forest and XGBoost, each with a few settings that keep it from memorising the training hours. Each predicts how much the level changes in the next hour.
Checked for overfitting: compared the chosen model's average error on the hours it learned from with its error on the test hours, allowing for some periods being harder to predict than others.

Counted the test hours where the prediction was within 20% of the real value. Readings below the 10th percentile were measured against that percentile, so tiny misses on near-zero readings don't count as big ones.
Flagged test hours where the miss was more than 51.11 µg/m³ (bigger than 95% of the misses on the validation period).
By design this limit flags 5% of the validation hours; on the test period it flagged 4.5% of hours. So the number of episodes partly depends on where the limit is set.

Grouped flagged hours that were less than 3 hours apart and checked each group: missing inputs or a gap, a stuck reading, or a sudden jump that nothing else shared mean a data problem; other pollutants moving the same way at the same time mean unusual pollution; anything else is unclear.
patterns: Most episodes peaked around 00:00, 20:00 and 21:00, and 72% fell on weekdays, about what you'd expect, so they are spread across the week. The busiest month was Nov 2016 with 31 episodes.
